content:
The objection goes like this. If Abraham and Ishmael built the Kaaba, why did the first Muslims pray towards Jerusalem? Turning their backs on God's own house makes no sense, unless the Mecca story came later.

The first thing to notice is where the critic learned that Muslims once faced Jerusalem. The qibla, the direction of prayer, is a matter of record in the Muslim sources, and those sources also give the reason for the change, the date, and the first reactions. The five points below set them out in order.

The second chapter of the Quran records it openly. It anticipates that foolish people will ask what turned the believers from their former direction of prayer, and answers that east and west belong to God.[1] It then instructs the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to turn his face towards the Sacred Mosque.[2]

The verse also records the Prophet's own longing: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face towards the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qibla with which you will be pleased."[2] The commentators explained that he hoped for the qibla of Abraham, and that he looked up to the sky waiting for the command. The text that is supposed to hide a later invention preserves the personal side of the change.

A fair reading adds a detail. The Quran says "the qibla they used to face" and does not name Jerusalem there. The identification comes from the hadith, the reports of the Prophet's words and actions, in which the Companion al-Bara ibn Azib says that the Prophet prayed towards Bayt al-Maqdis, the Holy House in Jerusalem, for sixteen or seventeen months.[3] The classical commentators name the questioners as the Jews of Medina, the hypocrites and the polytheists.

A later invention does not usually announce, in scripture, the very fact that would expose it.

The same passage says the earlier qibla was appointed to test who would follow the Messenger and who would turn on their heels.[4] The first direction was a test of obedience, and the change was one too. Muslims face a direction because they are told to. The stone is not what they worship.

The Quran presents the change as a test of the community's trust. People who had prayed one way for over a year were told to turn, and those who obeyed showed that their prayer was directed to God and not to a building. The commentators drew a lesson from it that Muslims still repeat: the believer follows the command, and the command can change while the One who gives it stays the same.

The verse goes on to say that God would never let the believers' faith be lost. Al-Bara reports why this was needed: some men had died, or had been killed, while the qibla was still Jerusalem, and the community asked what had become of their prayers.[3] Elsewhere in the same surah, righteousness is defined by belief in God and the last day and by good conduct, and the direction of the face is set aside as the measure.[5] The change therefore sits inside a passage that teaches what the direction is for, which is to give the community a common focus in worship.

Another verse in the same chapter makes the point in its widest form: "To God belong the east and the west. So wherever you turn, there is the face of God."[6] Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet prayed voluntary prayers on his mount while travelling, facing whichever way it went, and that the verse was revealed about that.[7] The direction of prayer is a command for the obligatory prayers, given for the unity of the community. It never implied that God is in one place more than another.

Facing Jerusalem put the first Muslims in the line of the prophets of Israel, whose sanctuary it was. The Quran names the farthest mosque, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, as a blessed place, and speaks of the sanctuaries that Solomon had made.[8] Its claim is continuity with that line, and then a return to the older house Abraham built.[9] Both directions sit inside the same story.

Facing Jerusalem in prayer was already the practice of the Jews. In the Bible, Solomon asks God to hear the prayers of his people when they pray towards the city and the house he has built, and Daniel in Babylon prays three times a day at a window open towards Jerusalem.[10] The first Muslims in Medina, living beside Jewish tribes, prayed in the same direction, which marked their faith as part of the same line of prophecy.

The sources also answer the question of which house is older. The Companion Abu Dharr asked the Prophet which mosque was first set up on earth. He replied, the Sacred Mosque, and then, the Farthest Mosque, and he said that forty years lay between them.[11] The chronology the critic wants is reversed in the Muslim account, in which Mecca comes first and Jerusalem second. The critic is right that a change of direction took place. The Muslim account makes it a return, and it is stated in the same surah that tells of Abraham raising the foundations of the House with Ishmael, a few pages before the change.

Muslim sources place the change around sixteen or seventeen months after the migration to Medina, which the sources date to the second year of the Hijra. The reports differ on the exact month.[12] It was public, contested, and remembered: a mosque in Medina is still called the Mosque of the Two Qiblas. Contested, public events are the kind of history that is hard to rewrite.

Several Companions report the event, among them al-Bara and Ibn Umar. Ibn Umar says that people were at Quba, on the edge of Medina, at the dawn prayer when a man came and told them that the Prophet had been commanded to face the Kaaba, and they turned in the middle of the prayer.[13] A story of this kind has the marks of a memory shared by a whole town. The scholars also differ on whether the Prophet had already faced Jerusalem while in Mecca, and some hold that he arranged his prayer there to face both the Kaaba and Jerusalem together. That disagreement was recorded openly, and nobody tidied it away.

The sources also name the mosque. The reports say the command came while the Prophet was leading a prayer among the clan of Banu Salima, and that he turned in the middle of it, which is why their mosque came to be called the Mosque of the Two Qiblas.[14] The details of the reports differ, as accounts of a single event told by different people usually do. They agree on the change, on its place in Medina and on its public character.

Some revisionist writers argue that early mosques point towards Petra, so Mecca must be a later substitute. A popular version of this appears in Dan Gibson's Qur'anic Geography.[15] The Quran, though, names Mecca in its own right, once as Bakka as the site of the first house for mankind and once as Makka, the valley in which the Prophet's party was restrained from the pilgrimage.[16]

Specialists in the history of astronomy and mosque orientation have rejected the Petra claim, pointing out that early Muslims had no precise way to compute the direction of Mecca over long distances and used a range of traditional methods, such as the rising and setting points of the sun and the position of stars.[17] The jurists went further: for those who cannot see the Kaaba, they held that the direction is what is required, and a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi says that what lies between east and west is qibla for the people of Medina.[18] Imprecise early orientations, leaning off the true bearing by differing amounts and in differing ways, are what you would expect, and they do not converge on Petra.

King answered Gibson in detail in a study titled "The Petra Fallacy", showing how medieval astronomers and builders actually determined the qibla and why the early mosques' orientations make sense as attempts to face Mecca with the methods available.[19] Several of the buildings Gibson cites also have uncertain dates or have been rebuilt, which weakens any argument from their present walls.

The strongest form of the revisionist case points to the Quran's description of Mecca and asks whether it fits the geography of the Hijaz. That question is taken up in the revisionist case weighed, which sets the archaeological and documentary evidence side by side.

The bottom line

The Quran records the first qibla, names the objection it would draw, and gives the reason. An objection that is quoted, anticipated and answered in the text it is aimed at has already been heard.

The evidence for the later-Mecca theory is the fact of the change itself, and that fact is recorded by the very community whose history is under attack, in a public event with many witnesses. The Quran names Mecca, the hadith place the change early in Medina, and the architectural case is weak. Face Jerusalem, then face Mecca: in both cases, the one being obeyed is the one who gave the command.

The change also gave the community a sign of its own identity. Facing the Kaaba connected the Muslims in Medina with the house of Abraham in the city they had left, and every Muslim who prays today, wherever they are, faces the same point. The qibla links each prayer to a history that the Quran traces back to Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundations of the House.
